134.title: Pradakshina
134.carry: keep the holy at the center
134.howItsDone: After darshan, many Hindus walk clockwise around the inner shrine of a temple, keeping the deity on their right, and some also circle sacred trees, the tulsi plant, or holy hills such as Arunachala; at home, some turn once in place at the end of puja.

segments.voice: Yesterday, darshan, and Dhruva opening his eyes. Your line was darshan is seeing god, and being seen.

Ganesha and his brother Kartikeya are told that whoever circles the world first wins. You met this race back on day twenty-five. Kartikeya jumps on his peacock and flies off across oceans and mountains. Ganesha, on his little mouse, simply walks around his parents, Shiva and Parvati, and says: you are my world. He wins. Children love that story. It's also a set of instructions, because Hindus walk around what they love all the time. Around shrines. Around trees. Around whole mountains. Today: pradakshina.
screen: `GANESHA CIRCLES HIS PARENTS.` → `YOU ARE MY WORLD.` → `TODAY: PRADAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: Pradakshina means walking around something holy, clockwise. The direction is inside the word: dakshina means the right hand, the right side. So you walk keeping the sacred on your right, the side of respect, with the center always in the center. After darshan at the front of the temple, many people turn and walk around the inner shrine, and many temples build a path for exactly this, a corridor that loops around the sanctum. Some people do one round, some three, some more, often a number that's meaningful to them or their family. It doesn't stop at the temple walls. People circle the sacred tulsi plant in the courtyard, or a great fig tree. Some circle whole mountains. At Arunachala, in Tamil Nadu, pilgrims walk all the way around the holy hill, many miles, often barefoot, often at night under the full moon. Even a Hindu wedding has a circle at its heart: the couple walks around the sacred fire. Why a circle? A straight line goes somewhere else. A circle keeps coming back to the same center. Every step, the holy is right there beside you, and you can't lose sight of it. And there's Ganesha's point: the thing you circle becomes your world. That's the teaching your feet are walking: in a Hindu life, God goes at the center, and everything else moves around it. At the end of home puja, when there's no room to walk, some people simply turn once in place, clockwise. The same act, made small. The center stays the center.
screen: `DAKSHINA: THE RIGHT SIDE.` · `A PATH AROUND THE SANCTUM.` · `TREES, FIRE, WHOLE MOUNTAINS.` · `GOD AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, and choose a center: a chair, a table, your corner, or just the spot where you were sitting. Walk slowly around it clockwise, keeping it on your right, one round, or three if there's room; with no room, turn once in place, and if walking is hard today, trace a slow circle with your hand. Then sit back down at the center.
Pradakshina. Walking clockwise around something holy, keeping it on your right, so the center stays the center. Today's word.
Your line: keep the holy at the center. Ganesha circled his parents and called them his world. Day one hundred thirty-four, done.

135.title: The priest and the hunter
135.hook: the temple priest, and the hunter whose love Shiva saw
135.carry: the priest offers the form; you bring the heart
135.howItsDone: In Hindu temples, the pujari performs the daily rites for the deity (bathing, dressing, food offerings and arti), and on request performs archana on a devotee's behalf, opening with a sankalpa that names the worshipper; the Tamil saint Kannappa, the hunter who offered his own eye, is honored at the Kalahasti temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pradakshina, walking around the holy. Your line was keep the holy at the center.
screen: `PRADAKSHINA — KEEP THE HOLY AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: In the hills of Kalahasti, in South India, the story goes, a temple priest came each morning to a lonely shrine of Shiva. He bathed the lingam, decorated it, chanted every verse exactly. And each morning he found a mess: his flowers pushed aside, meat left on the stone, the lingam wet with water someone had carried in their mouth. The someone was a young hunter named Thinnan. He knew no Sanskrit and no rules. He simply loved Shiva at first sight, and brought him what he had: water in his mouth, flowers from his own hair, the best meat from the hunt, tasted first. Today: the priest, and the hunter.
screen: `A PRIEST, A PERFECT RITE.` → `A HUNTER WITH NO RULES.` → `HE BRINGS WHAT HE HAS.`

segments.voice: Shiva told the heartbroken priest in a dream: hide, and watch. The next day the hunter came, and the priest saw blood running from one eye of the lingam. He cut out his own eye with an arrow and pressed it onto the bleeding one, and the bleeding stopped. Then the other eye began to bleed. He set his foot on the spot so he wouldn't lose it, and raised the arrow to his second eye. And Shiva's voice stopped him: stop, Kannappa. He's been Kannappa ever since, one of the sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva in the Periya Puranam. The story doesn't throw out the priest: Shiva showed him the hunter's love. The priest's word is pujari, the one who does the puja. In many temples only priests enter the inner shrine, and they care for the murti every day: bathing it, dressing it, feeding it, arti, by rules handed down for generations. And when you bring an offering, he makes it for you. He asks your name, often your family line, and sets them into the Sanskrit: who is offering, when, and why. That's the sankalpa. Then he recites the deity's names, often a hundred and eight, a flower with each: archana. The priest keeps the form exact, and the offering is still yours. You don't have to know every word. Kannappa didn't know one, and Shiva received what he brought. That love has a name: bhakti.
screen: `KANNAPPA GIVES HIS EYE.` · `STOP, KANNAPPA.` · `PUJARI — THE ONE WHO DOES THE PUJA.` · `SANKALPA, ARCHANA, AND YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Take one small thing within reach: a flower, a glass of water, a sweet, even a leaf. Hold it before your shrine, or just in front of you. Make your own sankalpa, in your own words: your name, today's date, and what you're offering it for. Then offer it, the way Kannappa did, with whatever you have. If you don't pray, say your name and one thing you'll give your whole heart to today, and set the thing down gently.
Pujari. The temple priest: he keeps the rites exact, and offers on your behalf, with your name inside. Today's word.
Your line: the priest offers the form; you bring the heart. Kannappa had only his heart. See you tomorrow.

screen: `THE PRIEST OFFERS THE FORM; YOU BRING THE HEART.` → `DAY 135 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TUKARAM AND THE BHAJAN.`

136.title: Tukaram and the bhajan
136.hook: devotional songs in everyday words, and the poet whose notebooks came back
136.howItsDone: Many Hindus gather in homes and temples, often weekly, to sing bhajans, simple devotional songs in regional languages, many by medieval poet-saints such as Tukaram and Mirabai, with harmonium, drums and small cymbals; Marathi warkari pilgrims sing Tukaram's abhangas on the walk to Pandharpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pujari and the hunter Kannappa. Your line was the priest offers the form; you bring the heart.

Almost four hundred years ago, beside the Indrayani river in Maharashtra, a shopkeeper named Tukaram was writing songs to God. Not in Sanskrit, the language of priests and scholars, but in Marathi, the language his neighbors spoke at the market. People sang them everywhere. Some learned men were furious: who was this shopkeeper, from a caste that wasn't supposed to teach scripture, to put sacred truths in street language? So, the story goes, Tukaram was told to sink his notebooks in the river. He did. Then he sat down on the bank and prayed, without eating, for thirteen days. Today: bhajan, and what came up out of the water.
screen: `A SHOPKEEPER'S SONGS TO GOD.` → `INTO THE RIVER.` → `THIRTEEN DAYS ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: On the thirteenth day, the tradition says, the notebooks rose to the surface, unharmed, and came back to him. Many tell it as a miracle. Some read it another way: the people carried the songs back, because they already knew them by heart. Either way, the songs lived. Tukaram's songs, called abhangas, are still sung by the warkaris, pilgrims who walk to the temple of Vitthala at Pandharpur every year, singing the whole way. That's the teaching in this story, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest: bhakti, devotion, belongs to everyone. Not only to people who know Sanskrit, or were born into the right family. The word bhajan comes from the same root as bhakti, your sixteenth word: bhaj, to share in, to adore. A bhajan is bhakti you can sing. Bhajans are simple: short lines, lots of repetition, in the languages people actually speak, Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Tamil and many more. Mirabai, the princess you met on day sixteen, sang hers for Krishna. One that many people know, sung at Gandhi's prayer meetings, begins: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram. Lord of the line of Raghu, King Ram; purifier of the fallen, Sita and Ram. And bhajans are usually sung together: a temple hall, or a living room with the sofas pushed back, a harmonium, a drum, tiny cymbals going ching, ching, and half the room off-key. Nobody's checking. The tradition doesn't ask for a pretty voice, or perfect Hindi. It asks for a whole one.
screen: `THE NOTEBOOKS CAME BACK.` · `BHAKTI BELONGS TO EVERYONE.` · `BHAJAN: BHAKTI YOU CAN SING.` · `NOT PRETTY. WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Sing the line, or sing it inside if you're somewhere you can't: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram. Once slowly, then a little louder than feels comfortable, without worrying about the tune or the pronunciation. If you'd rather, sing any song of devotion you know, in whatever language you actually speak. Then stop, and sit in the ringing quiet afterward.
Bhajan. A devotional song, simple and repeated, in everyday language, usually sung together: bhakti you can sing. Today's word.
Your line: bhakti belongs to every voice. Tukaram's songs came back up out of the river. That's day one hundred thirty-six.

137.title: The seven steps
137.hook: a wedding fire, a knotted scarf, stolen shoes, and a guest asking what's actually happening
137.carry: partners in dharma, friends by the seventh step
137.howItsDone: In many Hindu weddings the couple circle a sacred fire (the pheras) and take seven steps together (saptapadi) while a priest recites the vows; families differ on the number of circles and on customs like kanyadaan, the mangalsutra and sindoor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhajan, and Tukaram's songs that came back from the river. Your line was bhakti belongs to every voice. Today, the bhakti belongs to every voiceest thing a Hindu family ever throws, and the quiet steps in the middle of it.

A wedding hall, hour three. The couple sit under a canopy with a small fire between them and the priest. The groom's scarf has been knotted to the bride's sari. Two aunts are whispering about which way the knot should go. Near the door, the bride's cousins are hiding the groom's shoes and planning what to charge for them. And the groom's best friend, who didn't grow up with any of this, leans over and asks: what's actually happening? Plenty of people in that room couldn't tell him. Today: the steps in the middle.
screen: `A FIRE, A KNOTTED SCARF.` → `THE SHOES ARE MISSING.` → `WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING?`

segments.voice: The fire is Agni, and in the old wedding rites the fire is the witness. Everything important happens in front of it. When Sita married Rama, the Ramayana says, her father Janaka placed her hand in Rama's and said: this is Sita, my daughter, your partner in dharma; take her hand in yours. That's the Hindu idea of marriage in one line: two people walking dharma, the right way to live, together. In many weddings the couple walk around the fire, often seven times, in some communities four; these circles are the pheras. Inside or beside them is a rite called saptapadi: seven steps, taken together. An old household manual gives a wish for each step. One for food. Two for strength. Three for wealth. Four for happiness. Five for the herds, since this is a very old text. Six for the seasons. And at the seventh: with seven steps, be my friend. Partners in dharma, and at the last step, friends. Around it you'll see more, and families do these differently. Kanyadaan, the bride's parents placing her hand in the groom's, as Janaka did, which many families now do differently or reword. A mangalsutra, a necklace of black beads and gold, tied by the groom in many weddings. Sindoor, red powder, drawn into the parting of the bride's hair in many North Indian weddings. And the stolen shoes? That's joota chupai, a game, not a rite. The ransom is negotiable.
screen: `THE FIRE IS THE WITNESS.` · `PARTNERS IN DHARMA.` · `SEVEN STEPS, SEVEN WISHES.` · `AT THE SEVENTH: BE MY FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Seven breaths, seven steps. Think of someone who has walked beside you for a long time: a partner, a parent, a brother or sister, a friend. With each slow breath, take one step beside them in your mind: food, strength, wealth, happiness, the herds if you like, the seasons. On the seventh breath, just the word: friend, and sit quietly with them for a while.
Saptapadi. Seven steps, taken together before the fire, by partners in dharma; at the seventh, the couple are called friends. Today's word.
Your line: partners in dharma, friends by the seventh step. The last vow is the plainest one. Day one hundred thirty-seven.

138.title: Narada and the good company
138.hook: Narada's start as a servant boy, and the company of the true
138.carry: the company of the true changes you
138.howItsDone: Many Hindus attend satsangs, regular gatherings at temples, homes or community halls that usually include devotional singing, a reading or talk, silence and prasad, followed by tea and conversation; serving at them is part of the practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven steps around a wedding fire. Your line was partners in dharma, friends by the seventh step.

This week you went to the temple, walked around the shrine, met the priest, sang, and watched two people take seven steps. Under all of it: other people. Narada, the wandering sage who sings his way through every world, once told how he began. In a past life, he said, he was the small son of a maidservant. One year, as the rains came, a group of holy men arrived to stay where his mother worked, and the boy was sent to look after them. Today: satsang.
screen: `THIS WEEK: OTHER PEOPLE.` → `A MAIDSERVANT'S SMALL SON.` → `HOLY MEN, STAYING FOR THE RAINS.`

segments.voice: Every day of the rainy season, he brought the holy men water, swept up, and listened while they sang and talked about God. That's all. No vow, no books. He just stayed near people who loved God, and, the Bhagavata Purana says, the love rubbed off. Before they left, they taught him. That boy became Narada, who carries his veena through the worlds singing Vishnu's names, and who in the old stories turns up exactly when someone needs good company: he sheltered Prahlada's mother, and he set the boy Dhruva on his path. That's satsang, the word you met on day twenty. Sat means true, real, what actually is. Sang means company. Satsang is the company of the true, and in Hinduism it isn't just pleasant, it's a practice. Remember Shankara's chain from that day: good company leads to letting go, letting go to clarity, clarity to a steady mind, and a steady mind to freedom. Many follow a shape: singing, a reading or a short talk, silence, prasad, and tea afterward, which is where people become friends. Start with what's established and public: a temple, a long-running group, a friend's family. And good company welcomes you and lets you leave; a group that pressures you, asks for big money, or cuts you off from family isn't satsang. Sit in the back, sing what you can, stay for the tea. Narada started by carrying water.

139.title: Diwali begins: Narakasura's dawn
139.hook: five days of light begin: a clean house, something new, and a demon defeated before dawn
139.carry: light defeats darkness, and the captives go free
139.howItsDone: In the days before Diwali, many Hindu families clean their homes thoroughly; on Dhanteras they buy something new, often a metal utensil or coin, and light a lamp for Yama in the evening; on Naraka Chaturdashi many, especially in South India and Maharashtra, rise before dawn for an oil bath and new clothes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, satsang. Your line was the company of the true changes you.

A week before, it starts in the corners. Mothers and grandmothers pull everything off the shelves. Curtains washed, cupboards emptied, the dusty box under the bed finally dealt with. Kids grumbling. Then the shopping: a new steel pot, a silver coin, new clothes. Then patterns of colored powder on the doorstep. And finally the lamps, rows and rows of them on every windowsill and balcony, until the whole street glows. Now the practices become festivals. The biggest comes first. Today: Diwali.
screen: `THE HOUSE, TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.` → `A NEW POT, A SILVER COIN.` → `THEN, LAMPS ON EVERY SILL.`

segments.voice: You know the name by now: a row of lamps, your deepa from day one hundred and twelve, multiplied by a whole country. What's new is the calendar. Diwali falls in autumn, around the new moon, the darkest night of the month, usually in October or November. And for many families it's five days, not one; today, the first two. Different regions tell different stories. You met the one many North Indians tell on day sixty-nine: Rama coming home to Ayodhya, and the city lighting lamps to guide him. Jains and Sikhs mark their own observances in the same season. Day one is Dhanteras. Dhan means wealth, teras the thirteenth lunar day. The house has been cleaned, and now people buy something new, often metal: a pot, a spoon, a coin. In the evening, many families set one lamp outside, facing south, for Yama, the lord of death, asking him to pass the house by. Day two is Naraka Chaturdashi, the fourteenth. A demon king, Narakasura, had grown so cruel he'd imprisoned thousands. Krishna, and in many tellings his queen Satyabhama beside him, defeated him and set the prisoners free. In much of South India and Maharashtra, this is the big morning. People rise before dawn, rub their bodies with oil, bathe, put on new clothes, and the first firecrackers go off in the dark. That's the teaching at Diwali's heart, the one every region's story shares: light defeats darkness, and good frees what evil locked away. Many teachers read it inward too: the lamp is knowledge, the dark is ignorance. Clean house, clean body, and the darkest night is next.
screen: `FIVE DAYS, NOT ONE.` · `DHANTERAS: SOMETHING NEW.` · `NARAKASURA DEFEATED, PRISONERS FREED.` · `LIGHT DEFEATS DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Find one small cluttered thing within reach, a drawer, a desk corner, your phone's home screen, and take one minute to clear it, the way families clean before Diwali. Then, if you can, light a lamp or a candle, safely; if not, picture one on your front step, glowing outward into the dark street. If you pray, think of Krishna opening the prison doors; if not, just watch the light, and let it win.
Diwali. The festival of lamps, five days long: it begins with a clean house, something new, and a demon defeated before dawn. Today's word.

140.title: Diwali ends: the lifted hill
140.hook: a hill of food stacked before dawn: Lakshmi at the door, a mountain lifted, a sister's blessing
140.carry: krishna shelters everyone who comes under
140.howItsDone: On the new-moon night of Diwali many Hindu families perform Lakshmi puja with Ganesha, light lamps throughout the home and draw Lakshmi's footprints at the door; the next day temples offer annakut for Govardhan puja, and on Bhai Dooj sisters mark their brothers' foreheads with tilak and share a meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali began: Narakasura defeated before dawn. Your line was light defeats darkness, and the captives go free.

Before dawn, a temple kitchen is already roaring, while the lamps from the big night still smoke on the windowsills. Rice, lentils, vegetables, sweets, dish after dish, carried out in steel pans and stacked on the steps in front of the image until the food is shaped like a small hill. Children wait for their share and hear the story while they wait: a boy who once lifted a real hill. Across town, a sister is already planning tomorrow's plate for her brother. The lamps were only the middle of Diwali. Today, the last three days.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, A TEMPLE KITCHEN.` → `FOOD STACKED LIKE A HILL.` → `THE LAMPS WERE ONLY THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Day three is Lakshmi puja, on the new moon itself, the night you met on day eighty-eight: the clean house, the open door, the little footprints walking in. Ganesha is honored beside Lakshmi, and first, as always: clear the road, then begin. In Bengal it belongs to Kali, the fierce mother. Day four is Govardhan puja. In the Bhagavata Purana, young Krishna persuaded the cowherds of Vraj to honor their own hill, Govardhan, which fed their cows, instead of the storm god Indra. Indra, offended, sent rain for days. And Krishna lifted the whole hill with one hand, a single finger in many tellings, and held it up like an umbrella. Everyone fit underneath: the cowherds, the children, the cows. No one was turned away. Afterward, the story says, Indra came to ask forgiveness, and Krishna was honored with a name, Govinda. That's the teaching Govardhan puja keeps: God shelters whoever comes for refuge, and the food the earth gives is offered back with thanks. So temples build a mountain of food, called annakut, offer it, and share it with everyone. Day five is Bhai Dooj, for brothers and sisters. A sister marks her brother's forehead with a tilak, prays for his long life, and feeds him; he gives her a gift. Behind it: Yama, lord of death, visited his sister Yamuna on this day and was welcomed with a meal. Diwali opened with a lamp asking Yama to pass by. It closes with Yama as a brother, sitting down to eat.
screen: `LAKSHMI PUJA: GANESHA FIRST.` · `GOVARDHAN: THE HILL HELD UP.` · `SHELTER FOR EVERYONE.` · `BHAI DOOJ: A SISTER'S BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, set aside one small spoonful on a clean plate, the way annakut offers the food before anyone eats. If you pray, offer it with Krishna's name, Govinda; if not, simply thank whatever brought that food to you. Then wish a long life to someone who once sheltered you, the way a sister does on Bhai Dooj.
Diwali. Five days of light: something new, darkness defeated, Lakshmi welcomed on the darkest night, a hill lifted to shelter everyone, and siblings at the table. Today's word.
Your line: Krishna shelters everyone who comes under. Diwali's five days are done. See you tomorrow.
